findings.headline: You waive a fee most peers charge — and say nothing.
findings.body: Your non-network ATM fee is $0.00 against a $2.00 median across 13 peer banks (15th percentile, flagged as waived in our data). Add deposited-item returns at $5 versus a $15 median (15th percentile) and you have two genuinely customer-friendly lines that competitors' own published schedules would substantiate as marketing claims. Today, neither appears in any.

findings.headline: Your entire penalty-fee suite is invisible to comparison.
findings.body: NSF, overdraft, overdraft-protection transfer, and monthly maintenance — the four categories regulators and comparison sites watch most closely — did not appear in your published schedule data. Peers publish these lines (NSF median $12, overdraft median $31). Until you do, the most scrutinized part of your pricing is a blank that others fill in for you.

findings.headline: Small premiums sit on the money-movement side.
findings.body: Outgoing domestic wires ($25 vs a $20 median, 80th percentile) and cashier's checks ($10 vs $8, 89th percentile) run modestly above the cohort. The dollar gaps are small — $5 and $2 — but they land on business and higher-balance customers, the segment most likely to compare schedules line by line.

exec_narrative: Net position: Forbright Bank's published schedule is customer-friendly where it is visible — a waived non-network ATM fee, deposited-item returns at a third of the peer median, incoming wires below market — with only minor premiums on outgoing wires and cashier's checks. The defining feature, though, is what is missing: the entire penalty-fee suite (NSF, overdraft, OD-protection transfer, monthly maintenance) is absent from the published data, so the categories that draw the most scrutiny are the ones where you cannot be benchmarked — or defended. The agenda is short: publish the missing lines, decide the two small wire-side premiums, and start claiming credit for the fees you already waive.

callouts.title: Waived non-network ATM fee — $0.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $2.00 · 15th percentile · n=13 · flagged: waived
callouts.body: Most peers charge for using another institution's ATM; you don't. This is precisely the kind of everyday, high-frequency fee customers notice — and the kind of claim ('we never charge you to use an ATM') that peer schedules substantiate. A waived fee that nobody knows about is a cost without a benefit; advertised, it becomes acquisition copy.

callouts.title: Unpublished penalty suite — NSF, overdraft, OD transfer, maintenance
callouts.stat: 4 of 15 benchmark categories flagged as data gaps · peer medians: NSF $12.00 · overdraft $31.00 · OD transfer $5.00 · maintenance $10.00
callouts.body: In your cohort the NSF median has fallen to $12 and a quarter of peers charge $5 or less — a favorable environment to publish into if your pricing is competitive, and a risk to surface deliberately if it is not. Either way, leaving the most scrutinized fee categories unpublished means examiners, journalists, and comparison sites encounter them on their terms rather than yours.

callouts.title: Outgoing domestic wire — $25.00
callouts.stat: Peer median $20.00 · 80th percentile · n=15 — Cashier's check $10 vs $8 median (P89, n=9)
callouts.body: Two service lines price in the top quintile of the cohort. The amounts are small, but wires and official checks are disproportionately used by business and high-balance customers — the relationships with the most alternatives. At $5 and $2 over median, these fees earn little and sit at the top of the distribution.

callouts.title: Deposited item return — $5.00 vs a $15.00 median
callouts.body: When a customer deposits a check that bounces, you charge a third of what the median peer does — against the broadest peer sample in your pack. Paired with the waived ATM fee and below-market incoming wires ($10 vs $15), this rounds out a receiving-side fee posture that is quietly among the friendliest in the cohort.

context_narrative:
Two currents define the fee landscape your schedule competes in. First, the retreat from NSF: large banks have largely eliminated returned-item fees, and the pressure has migrated down-market — visible in your own cohort, where the published NSF median has fallen to $12 and a quarter of peers charge $5 or less. Second, published fee schedules have become marketing documents: public, scraped, and compared, which turns every waived fee into an unclaimed asset and every unpublished line into an open question others answer for you.

Community-scale institutions ($1B–$10B) occupy the exposed middle: large enough to be included in comparisons and examiner conversations, without the brand gravity that lets money-center banks price quietly. For a bank whose visible schedule already skews customer-friendly, the highest-leverage moves are not cuts — they are disclosure and storytelling: publish the penalty suite on your own terms, trim or justify the two wire-side premiums, and put the fees you already waive to work in your marketing.
